Overview
Sports-related injuries account for approximately 5.3 million healthcare visits annually.
Although less common than extremity injuries, spinal injuries are among the most
feared injuries because of the potential for catastrophic disability (Resources 1 and 2).
Sports-related spine injuries range from simple contusions and muscular strains to
fractures with and without spinal cord injuries. Compared with the general population,
athletes place substantially greater loads on the lumbar spine, including repetitive
flexion, extension, and axial loads. A higher incidence of degenerative disk changes have
been noted in elite athletes, most commonly at the L5-S1 level.
Epidemiology
Sports-related spine injuries vary by country and sport participation.
Worldwide, the highest risk of spinal cord injury has been noted in diving, skiing, rugby,
horseback riding, and American football (Resources 3 through 5)

Epidemiology
Epidemiologic data related to sports-related spine and spinal cord injuries vary by
country and sport participation. The sports associated with the highest risk of spinal cord
injury worldwide include diving, skiing, rugby, horseback riding, and American football.
Although cervical spine injuries are more frequently associated with these sports,
lumbar spine injuries are common. In American football, lumbar spine injuries are more
common because of blocking and are most likely to occur in offensive linemen. Of all the
lumbar spine injuries associated with skiing and snowboarding, transverse and spinal

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Lumbar Sprains/Strains
Injuries that result from stretching or overloading a muscle. A specific event often is recalled.

Lumbar Sprains/Strains
Soft-tissue injuries result from stretching or overloading a muscle, and athletes often
recall a specific event that caused the injury. A delay in symptom onset may occur
because of inflammation. Management involves rest, active and passive exercises, and
NSAIDs.
Lumbar Disk Herniation
Disk herniations may occur because of weakness in the posterolateral portion of the annulus
fibrosus.
Pain results from direct mechanical compression and chemical irritation of a nerve root.
Herniations most commonly occur at L4-L5 or L5-S1 and with repetitive flexion and
compression movements.

Lumbar Disk Herniation
Lumbar disk herniations may result from fissures in the weaker posterolateral portion of
the annulus fibrosus, subsequently allowing disk components to herniate into the spinal
canal resulting in pain, numbness, and/or weakness in the extremities (Resource 6). Pain
results from direct mechanical compression of the nerve root and from chemical
irritation of the nerve root by substances within the nucleus pulposus. Herniations most

disk herniations in athletes most commonly occur in those younger than 35 years and

Patients commonly report prodromal low back pain followed by radicular pain that may
be associated with a neurologic deficit (Figure 1). Symptoms are provoked by sitting,
walking, standing, coughing, or sneezing and may improve by lying supine with a pillow
under the legs or lying on the side in a fetal position.

Spondylolysis is a stress reaction that leads to a defect of the pars interarticularis.
It most commonly occurs at L5 because of excessive repetitive loading stresses, often
repetitive hyperextension and twisting forces.
Approximately 85% of pars defects are bilateral and more likely to progress to
spondylolisthesis.2

Spondylolysis
Spondylolysis is a stress reaction that leads to a defect (osteolysis or fracture) of the pars
interarticularis. It is relatively common, affecting as many as 50% of young athletes who
present with low back pain.2 The pars interarticularis is a narrow isthmus of bone
connecting the superior and inferior lumbar facets. Spondylolysis most commonly
occurs at L5 because of a decreased distance between the L4 inferior facet and the S1
superior facet, resulting in excessive repetitive loading stresses on the L5 pars
interarticularis. Spondylolysis is commonly associated with increased training volume
and sports that involve repetitive hyperextension and twisting forces applied to the
lumbar spine, such as soccer, gymnastics, and American football. Approximately 85% of
pars defects are bilateral, which are more likely to progress to spondylolisthesis than
unilateral defects. This can be classified as acute and non-united stress fracture. The
acute bone stress category can be pre-spondylolysis, stress reaction, or stress fracture.
Pre-spondylolysis abnormalities usually are asymptomatic, with radiographic evidence of
bone stress with no fracture line. Stress reactions are similar to those of pre-
spondylolytic bone stress but are symptomatic, whereas stress fractures involve cortical
disruption. Non-united stress fractures can be categorized into early, progressive, and
terminal phases. The early phase usually involves a hairline fracture, the progressive
involves a wider fracture, and the terminal phase involves a fracture with chronic
sclerotic pseudoarthrosis.
Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolisthesis is defined as the translation of one vertebral body in relation to an adjacent
body.

Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolisthesis is the translation of one vertebral body in relation to an adjacent body.
Five main types of spondylolisthesis exist. Types I and II are the most common. Type I
(dysplastic) occurs secondary to developmental defects, whereas type II (isthmic) occurs
secondary to pars defects and is subdivided based on the integrity of the pars
interarticularis. Type IIA is a defect secondary to a stress fracture as previously described

Lumbar Spine Fractures
Lumbar spine fractures most commonly result from lower-energy trauma or repetitive activity,
and may result from axial loads, hyperextension or hyperflexion, rotation, or direct trauma.
The posterior ligamentous complex is important for the overall stability of the spinal column.

Lumbar Spine Fractures
Lumbar spine fractures are minor injuries that result from lower-energy trauma;
repetitive activity; or, rarely, major fractures associated with instability and/or neurologic
deficit (Resource 7). Spinal fractures may result from axial loads, hyperextension or
hyperflexion, rotation, or direct trauma. Fractures that involve only one column of the
spine, such as vertebral body compression fractures, generally are considered stable
and only require symptomatic management. Major fractures, such as burst fractures or
fracture-dislocations, primarily are associated with collision sports and may require
surgical fixation for stability. The posterior ligamentous complex is important for the
overall stability of the spinal column by preventing excessive translation, rotation,
flexion, or distraction. It consists of facet joint capsules, the interspinous ligament, the
supraspinous ligament, and the ligamentum flavum.
Injury Classification
Disk Herniations
Herniations are described based on their anatomic location and their morphology.
Central: may not cause substantial radiculopathy but causes low back pain
Posterolateral/subarticular: compresses the traversing nerve root

Burst Fractures
Burst fractures involve the entire vertebral body with varying degrees of bony retropulsion into
the spinal canal and result from high-energy trauma involving a direct axial load with a forward
bending movement.
Approximately 15% of patients also have a noncontiguous spinal fracture elsewhere, and
approximately 50% of patients have a neurologic deficit.
Stability is determined by the integrity of the posterior ligamentous structures, facet capsule
height, and degree of kyphosis.
Radiographs should be obtained in the supine position because of acute traumatic injury.
CT best demonstrates bony retropulsion.

Burst Fractures
Fractures characterized as burst fractures involve the entire vertebral body, including
both anterior and posterior cortices, and varying degrees of bony retropulsion into the
spinal canal. These result from high-energy trauma involving a direct axial load in
combination with a forward bending movement. Common mechanisms of injury include
motor vehicle collisions, falls from a height, and direct trauma from a heavy falling
object. Burst fractures most commonly occur in younger men, with the L1 being the
vertebra most frequently affected. In approximately 15% of patients, a noncontiguous
fracture is located elsewhere in the spinal column. In addition, a neurologic deficit is
present in approximately 50% of patients; therefore, a careful neurologic examination,
including assessment of rectal tone, is important to rule out conus medullaris or a spinal
cord injury. A stable burst fracture has intact posterior ligamentous structures
(interspinous and supraspinous ligaments) and facet capsules with less than 20% height
loss or 20° of local kyphosis.3,4
AP and lateral radiographs should be obtained with the patient in the supine position
because of the acute traumatic injury (Figure 4). Spinous processes splaying apart
should increase concern for a potential burst fracture. CT is the preferred imaging
modality because axial CT scans best show bony retropulsion into the spinal canal and
sagittal CT scans show vertebral body height loss and any interspinous widening or facet
subluxation/dislocation (Figure 5). Although MRI is not as helpful in the diagnosis of

Compression Fractures
Compression fractures involve only the anterior aspect of the vertebral body without bony
retropulsion and commonly result from a compressive or flexion force.
Radiographs demonstrate a wedge-shaped fracture and may demonstrate vertebral body
height loss. MRI characterizes the edematous changes indicative of acute injury.

Compression Fractures

Compression fractures occur if the anterior aspect of the vertebral body fails under a
compressive or flexion force while the posterior aspect, including the posterior vertebral
wall, remains intact. These fractures usually result from low-energy trauma, and patients
remain neurologically intact because no retropulsion of bone into the spinal canal
occurs.
Lateral radiographs aid in establishing the diagnosis because the wedged shape of the
compression fracture can be visualized (Figure 6). AP radiographs may appear normal or
demonstrate a subtle loss of vertebral body height. T2-weighted MRIs are useful to
characterize the edematous changes under the fractured end plate that would be
indicative of an acute injury. In addition, marrow replacement processes or posterior
vertebral wall retropulsion may be observed. CT is useful to rule out bony retropulsion
into the spinal canal and, therefore, rule out burst fracture (Figure 7). CT is indicated if
MRI cannot be obtained. Bone scintigraphy may be useful to classify the age of a fracture
(acute, subacute, or chronic); however, bone scintigraphy is principally indicated to
identify occult injuries or plan surgical management.

Transverse Process Fractures
Transverse process fractures are avulsion-type injuries caused by severe contractions of the
attached muscle and may result from blunt abdominal trauma or a direct blow to the back.
Approximately 50% of patients have associated intra-abdominal organ injuries.5

These fractures may be easily missed on radiographs because of overlapping shadows.
CT is helpful to identify subtle fractures.

Transverse Process Fractures
The transverse process arises from the junction of the pedicles and lamina and projects
laterally and posteriorly. It is the attachment site for the quadratus lumborum and the
aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis, and fractures may result from severe
contractions of these muscles. These are described as avulsion-type fractures, with as
many as 50% of patients having associated intra-abdominal organ injuries. Common
mechanisms of injury include blunt abdominal trauma or a direct blow to the back, such
as that which occurs during a football injury or during a fall while snowboarding.5 These
are considered stable injuries and often require no specific management; however;
nonunion may occur in patients with constant pulling of the attached muscles.
AP and lateral radiographs are obtained initially; however, transverse process fractures
may be easily missed (Figure 8). CT is preferred for diagnosis and may help identify
other subtle fractures, especially in the thoracic spine, a location in which radiographs
may be difficult to interpret because of overlapping shadows. MRI is not indicated unless
signs of nerve root irritation are present.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
A thorough evaluation of the patient’s presentation, symptoms, and underlying pathology
should be performed.
Thorough questioning and examination should be performed to assess for possible spinal
cord dysfunction.
Discogenic pain often presents as a diffuse, band-like distribution, whereas facet-mediated
pain often is localized and worse with activity.
Assessment for nonorganic sources of pain also is important because these may affect the
patient’s pain score and overall response to treatment.


Patient History
Low back pain is the most common symptom for which patients seek medical care. A
timeline for a patient’s symptoms should be established; the nature, duration, onset,
and aggravating and alleviating factors should be identified; and symptoms should be
characterized. A focus should be placed on any inciting event and the presence or
absence of red flag symptoms that may indicate a possible underlying pathology
requiring a timely and focused workup. Clumsiness, gait instability, bowel/bladder
dysfunction, or sexual dysfunction should alert a physician to assess for causes of spinal
cord dysfunction.6 Discogenic pain may be worse with flexion, sitting, or prolonged axial
loading and often is described in a diffuse, band-like distribution. Facet-mediated pain
may be worse with extension, often is activity-related, and generally is well-localized.
The physician also should be aware of possible indications for nonorganic sources of
pain, which can be evaluated via the Waddell signs. These signs consist of tenderness,
simulation, distraction, regional disturbances, and overreaction.6 The presence of at
least three of these signs should prompt the physician to assess for possible nonorganic
sources of pain. Although the Waddell signs do not eliminate the possibility of a true
spinal problem, they are associated with high pain scores and overall poorer treatment
outcomes.
Physical Examination
Inspection, palpation, range of motion, and a neurologic examination should be performed.
The nature of a patient’s symptoms may help determine the areas of the physical examination
process that should be emphasized.

Physical Examination
Every physical examination of a new patient should include components of inspection,
palpation, range of motion, and neurologic evaluation (Resource 8). Depending on
various factors, including presenting symptoms, differential diagnosis, prior imaging

Lumbar Sprains/Strains

Lumbar Sprains/Strains
Tenderness to palpation is elicited within the paraspinal musculature, with possible
associated muscle spasms. Pain can be reproduced with flexion and extension
movements or decreased range of motion may be present secondary to pain. Swelling at
the site of injury may occur in patients who sustain direct trauma resulting in a
contusion injury. Pain does not radiate below the knee, and neurologic examination is
normal.
Lumbar Disk Herniation
Deep tendon reflexes and manual muscle testing may help localize a lesion if herniation is
suspected.
Evaluation of dural tension signs also may aid in localizing a herniation lesion.
Cauda equina syndrome is rare; however, if suspected, a rectal tone examination should be
considered.
Hyporeflexia is expected in patients with lumbar radiculopathy.
Decreased patellar reflex: L4 radiculopathy (50% sensitivity, 83% sensitivity)7
Decreased Achilles tendon reflex: S1 radiculopathy (48% sensitivity, 83% sensitivity)7
Normal reflexes may be present in the hyperacute setting.
L3 radiculopathy: weakness with hip adduction (67% sensitivity, 40% specificity)
L4 radiculopathy: weakness with knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion (46% sensitivity, 70%
specificity)
L5 radiculopathy: weakness with hip abduction, extensor hallucis longus
Extensor hallucis longus weakness may be the only sign to confirm L5 radiculopathy and
must be assessed (54% sensitivity, 64% specificity).

Dural tension signs8
Straight leg raise (SLR)—Evaluates for irritation of the L5 or S1 nerve root and can be
performed in the seated (in which case it is referred to as a slump test) or supine position.
Pain and paresthesia reproduced in the affected limb with 30° to 70° of hip flexion. The
sensitivity and specificity for the SLR is 64% and 53%, respectively.
Contralateral SLR—Pain and paresthesia reproduced in the affected limb with 30° to 70° of
hip flexion of the unaffected limb. Less sensitive, but more specific than the SLR (29%
sensitivity, 89% specificity).
Femoral nerve stretch test—Assesses for nerve root irritation in the high lumbar region, L2-3,
and L3-4. Anterior thigh pain and paresthesia reproduced with passive knee flexion and hip
extension.

Lumbar Disk Herniation
Discogenic pain related to herniation is worse with flexion, while sitting, or with
prolonged axial loading and often will be described as a diffuse, band-like distribution.
Deep tendon reflexes should be assessed if concern for lumbar disk herniation and
radiculopathy exists. Manual muscle testing will help localize nerve roots that may be
affected (33% sensitivity, 83% specificity).7
Although rare, cauda equina syndrome may be ruled out by assessing for the classic
constellation of saddle anesthesia, bilateral (occasionally unilateral) lower extremity
motor and sensory deficits, and acute bowel/bladder dysfunction.
Spondylolysis/Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis often is asymptomatic, whereas spondylolisthesis commonly presents as back
pain of insidious onset. In patients with an acute pars interarticularis fracture, pain often is
associated with high-intensity activities.
Radiculopathy is uncommon unless spondylolisthesis results in foraminal stenosis.

The L5 nerve root is most commonly affected, and patients may present with subtle extensor
hallucis longus or hip external rotation weakness.
Hamstring tightness and subsequent decreased popliteal angle may result from chronic
postural changes.
Palpable step-offs are associated with high-grade spondylolisthesis.

Spondylolysis/Spondylolisthesis
Spondylolysis is most commonly asymptomatic and may be incidentally observed on
radiographs, whereas spondylolisthesis most commonly presents as back pain of
insidious onset (Figure 9), except in patients with an acute pars interarticularis fracture
(Figure 10). In the acute setting, pain is present with activity, most frequently increasing
with high-intensity activity, and improves with rest. Low-level pain always may be
present in the chronic setting. Radiculopathy is uncommon, and true nerve compression
tests are rare; however, if spondylolisthesis results in foraminal stenosis, then
radiculopathy often is bilateral into the buttocks or the posterior thigh. The one-legged
hyperextension test, commonly referred to as the stork test, can be used to evaluate
spondylolysis. To perform the test, the patient stands on one leg facing away from the
examination while extending the lumbar spine. The test is positive if the patient has pain
in the lumbar spine on the same side as the weight-bearing leg (50% to 73% sensitivity,
17% to 32% specificity).9

Rehabilitation
Although not mandatory, many physicians recommend physical therapy and similar
rehabilitation techniques to help patients return to activity.40,76,77 This can be achieved
via formal physical therapy or via a home-based exercise program monitored by the
clinician; however, in patients with severe symptoms or patients not improving via a
home-based regimen, referral to a knowledgeable physical therapist may be beneficial.
Although no specific rehabilitation exercise protocol exists, the general consensus
focuses on increasing core, pelvic, and gluteal strength and hamstring flexibility if
underlying tightness is identified. As patients progress through a prescribed program,
the exercises become more challenging given that the patient can perform them without
pain.
Evidence pertaining to the nonsurgical management of spondylolysis and
spondylolisthesis is extremely limited, and the main approaches used primarily are
based on observational studies and clinical experience. Limited evidence supports the
use of physical therapy to manage spondylolysis.40,77,78 Studies on rehabilitation have
rarely distinguished among spondylolysis types or specified the type of physical therapy
program used;40,77 however, a number of studies support physical therapy in these
patients.79-82
Outcomes
In general, return to play after lumbar spine injury depends on the resolution of symptoms,
restoration of complete range of motion, and demonstration of sport-specific movements in a
practice environment without recurrent symptoms.

Lumbar Disk Herniation
The overall prognosis of patients with a lumbar disk herniation is favorable, with one
large study demonstrating successful return to play in 82% of athletes.33 Most athletes
can be successfully treated via nonsurgical techniques consisting of early activity, core-
strengthening protocols, and a gradual return to sport-specific activity.2 A large study
evaluating athletes in the NFL, National Hockey League, Major League Baseball, and
National Basketball Association showed an equivalent return to play after surgical
management (mean, 80%) compared with nonsurgical management. NFL players with a
lumbar disk herniation who underwent surgical treatment had greater career longevity
(36 games played) compared with those treated nonsurgically (20 games played).
Outcome measures fail to improve with nonsurgical treatment continued for more than
6 weeks in patients with spine pathology confirmed on imaging studies.33,83 Multiple
systematic reviews have failed to demonstrate a consistent benefit of any single surgical
technique over another.84-86 The Spine Patients Outcomes Research Trial showed that
patients who underwent surgical treatment had improvements in all primary outcome
measures at 2, 4, and 8 years postoperatively and better outcomes in patients who
underwent surgical treatment within 6 months of symptom onset. Subgroup analysis
showed that preoperative epidural steroid injection did not influence surgical outcome,
and that obesity was associated with a lower clinical benefit with surgical and
nonsurgical management.87-91

Spondylolysis
In patients treated nonsurgically for spondylolysis and grade I spondylolisthesis, 83.9%
had satisfactory results based on clinical and radiographic evidence. No outcome
difference was noted based on whether patients were treated with the use of a brace.
Unilateral defects heal considerably better than bilateral defects, and acute defects heal
more often than subacute or chronic defects.92 Athletes who ceased sports activities for
3 months after diagnosis were 16 times more likely to experience excellent resolution of
symptoms.34 With chronic defects, 91% of athletes with radiographically negative, bone
scans positive for spondylolysis for a mean of 9 years reported good to excellent low
back functional outcomes at final follow-up despite the absence of healing observed on
radiographs.35 Variety surgical techniques are available, and, recently, direct pars
interarticularis repair with débridement and interlaminar screw fixation has gained
favor. Of patients who underwent direct interlaminar screw repair with the use of iliac
crest autograft, 90% reported decreased postoperative visual analog scale scores, and
76% of the competitive athletes returned to their respective sports.93

Adolescents with high-grade spondylolisthesis who are asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic
can be treated nonsurgically.
Patients treated surgically and nonsurgically have similar long-term outcomes.
Higher slip angles are associated with poorer long-term results regardless of treatment

Spondylolisthesis
High-grade spondylolisthesis in young athletes who are asymptomatic or mildly
symptomatic can be managed nonsurgically without risk of neurologic problems.37
Surgical treatment may be considered in athletes with recurrent symptoms after bracing,
persistent pain for at least 6 months, pain that precludes return to sports activity, or
progressive spondylolisthesis (greater than 50% slip). Although return to play is possible
6 to 12 months postoperatively, patients should be counseled that lumbar fusion may be
a career-ending treatment option because many surgeons allow return to noncontact
sports only.2,6 Patients treated surgically have long-term results similar to those of
patients treated nonsurgically. Regardless of the treatment method, patients with higher
slip angles have poorer long-term outcomes than patients with lower slip angles.37

Mixed evidence exists regarding bracing for the management of lumbar spine fractures.
Patients with nonsurgically managed burst fractures and an intact posterior ligamentous
complex have better functional outcomes than patients treated surgically.

ligamentous complex who were treated nonsurgically reported less pain and better
functional outcomes at long-term follow-up than patients treated surgically.94
